title: Why Subliminal Learning Needs So Much Data: A Noisy Inverse View through Steering Vector Recovery

paper.title: Why Subliminal Learning Needs So Much Data: A Noisy Inverse View through Steering Vector Recovery
paper.abstract:
Abstract Subliminal learning lets a student inherit a teacher’s behavioral trait from
semantically unrelated data, yet published demonstrations typically require
tens of thousands of carrier examples. We ask where this data requirement
comes from. Our testbed is subliminal steering: the teacher trait is a known
residual-stream vector Δ T \Delta_{T} , so transfer can be measured directly as
parameter recovery. On identical carrier prefixes, we compare token-level
(hard) NLL supervision with full-distribution (soft) KL supervision. At
initialization the two objectives give nearly collinear gradients, and both
align poorly with Δ T \Delta_{T} . Under iterative optimization, however, they
diverge: soft supervision recovers Δ T \Delta_{T} almost exactly from a few hundred
carriers, while hard supervision stays well below it even with tens of
thousands. We explain this gap by casting steering-vector distillation as a
noisy linear inverse problem. Locally, the carrier task maps the trait through
its Fisher matrix F F , so gradients point toward F ​ Δ T F\Delta_{T} rather than Δ T \Delta_{T} . Gradient descent then acts as a progressively less-damped inverse
of F F . With soft targets, this inverse restores low-curvature directions.
With hard labels, it also amplifies the sampling noise in
those same directions. The result is an optimal inversion depth that grows
with the number of independent carriers. Experiments on Qwen2.5-7B and
Gemma-2-9B confirm four predictions: the Fisher distortion of the initial
gradient, recovery ordered from steep to flat directions, an optimal depth
that shifts with data scale, and the finding that resampling completions from
a fixed prompt pool works as well as adding new prompts. In this setting,
large carrier datasets are needed less to reveal the trait than to suppress
label noise amplified by Fisher inversion. Code is available at https://github.com/luoyuchenmlcv/subliminal-data .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Model distillation trains a student to imitate a teacher’s outputs ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) . Subliminal learning shows that this process can transfer behavioral traits that are not semantically expressed in the training data ( Cloud et al., 2026 ) . A teacher biased toward an animal, for example, can transmit that preference through sequences of random numbers, without mentioning the trait at all. Subliminal transfers have also been observed across carrier tasks, model families, and trait types ( Cloud et al., 2026 ; Schrodi et al., 2025 ; Blank et al., 2026 ; Morgulis and Hewitt, 2026 ) . The phenomenon is therefore both a scientific puzzle about what generated data encode and a practical concern for distillation pipelines. Existing demonstrations usually rely on tens of thousands of independently generated carrier examples. Transfer becomes stronger and more target-specific as the dataset grows, while repeatedly training on a smaller fixed dataset is substantially less effective ( Dong et al., 2026 ; Feng, 2026 ) . This dependence admits two candidate explanations. Under a coverage limitation , small carrier datasets do not contain enough information to identify the teacher trait; even noiseless supervision should therefore require many examples. Under a noise limitation , the trait is already identifiable from a much smaller carrier set, but sampled hard targets provide a noisy estimate of the teacher distribution; replacing them with distributional supervision should substantially improve the learning signal or its final recovery. Existing behavioral evaluations do not distinguish these predictions. We test these explanations in the subliminal-steering framework ( Morgulis and Hewitt, 2026 ) . The teacher trait is represented by a known residual-stream vector Δ T \Delta_{T} , and the student learns a vector Δ S \Delta_{S} from carrier data generated by the steered teacher. Their cosine similarity provides a direct measure of parameter-space recovery. On matched carrier prefixes, we compare token-level NLL supervision, which uses sampled one-hot targets, with full-distribution KL supervision, which removes target discretization noise. We examine this intervention at two levels. Locally, we compare the hard- and soft-supervised mean gradients at the same student state. Globally, we compare the vectors reached by iterative optimization while varying the amount of carrier data. The results create a two-sided contradiction. With sufficiently many carriers, the hard- and soft-supervised mean gradients are nearly collinear, yet both have similarly low alignment with Δ T \Delta_{T} . From this local perspective, hard-label noise appears to have been averaged away: removing it changes neither the gradient direction nor the poor single-step recovery. Iterative optimization gives the opposite impression. Distributional supervision recovers Δ T \Delta_{T} almost perfectly from only hundreds of examples, showing that large-scale carrier coverage is unnecessary in this controlled setting. Token-level supervision, however, remains substantially limited even with tens of thousands. Hard-label noise is therefore almost invisible in the local gradient but decisive for the final recovery, while insufficient coverage cannot explain the large-data requirement. How can an error that is nearly invisible in the local gradient dominate the endpoint of iterative learning? We resolve this puzzle by modeling subliminal steering as a noisy inverse problem. Under a local linear approximation, the hard-supervised descent direction at optimization step k k satisfies − g ^ N hard ​ ( Δ S ( k ) ) ≈ F ⁡ ( Δ T − Δ S ( k ) ) − ξ ¯ N , Cov ⁡ ( ξ ¯ N ) ≈ F N , -\widehat{g}_{N}^{\text{hard}}\!\left(\Delta_{S}^{(k)}\right)\approx F\!\left(\Delta_{T}-\Delta_{S}^{(k)}\right)-\overline{\xi}_{N},\qquad\operatorname{Cov}(\overline{\xi}_{N})\approx\frac{F}{N}, (1) where F F is the carrier Fisher matrix, N N is the number of supervised completion tokens, and ξ ¯ N \overline{\xi}_{N} is zero-centered discretization noise; distributional supervision removes this term. At initialization and large N N , both objectives are dominated by F ​ Δ T F\Delta_{T} : their gradients are therefore nearly identical, but the Fisher transformation can make both poorly aligned with Δ T \Delta_{T} . Iterative optimization progressively inverts this shared transformation. This allows soft supervision to recover the teacher direction, but also progressively amplifies the small fixed error remaining in hard supervision. Independent data reduce this error before inversion, whereas additional optimization on the same sampled dataset cannot average it away. Our contributions are three conclusions from this noisy-inverse model: 1. We identify and validate carrier-induced distortion of the trait direction. Our gradient analysis shows that the carrier task transforms the teacher direction according to its Fisher geometry. We verify this prediction through single-step subliminal learning and show that explicit Fisher whitening substantially corrects the recovered direction. 2. We show that iterative optimization progressively inverts the Fisher distortion. Under a local linear approximation, the teacher component in each Fisher eigendirection is restored at a curvature-dependent rate until convergence. We validate this predicted dynamics empirically: with distributional-level supervision, Δ S \Delta_{S} ultimately recovers Δ T \Delta_{T} with near-perfect alignment. 3. We show that data scale controls reliable inversion depth. Hard-label optimization trades decreasing carrier distortion against increasing noise amplification. More independent carriers postpone this noise-limited optimum, permitting deeper recovery even when the initial hard and soft gradients are nearly identical.

sections.heading: 3 Empirical Puzzle: Locally Indistinguishable Signals, Divergent Recovery
sections.text: The coverage and noise hypotheses make different predictions about distributional supervision. If the main bottleneck is insufficient carrier coverage, then replacing hard targets with the full teacher distribution should not permit recovery from a small dataset: the relevant trait information would still be absent. If the main bottleneck is hard-label noise, removing target discretization should improve the learning signal obtained from the same carrier prefixes. We test both predictions in the controlled steering-vector setting. We first compare the local learning signals. At the common state Δ S = 0 \Delta_{S}=0 , we compute the full-data descent directions from hard NLL and soft KL on matched carrier prefixes. Across model–trait pairs, their mutual cosine is close to one. Nevertheless, both directions have similarly low alignment with Δ T \Delta_{T} and produce weak norm-matched trait expression (Figure 1 ). Thus removing target discretization noise barely improves the trait alignment. Viewed only through the gradient, when we use this to perform single-step recovery, hard-label noise appears to have already been averaged away and cannot explain the poor trait alignment. Figure 1: Hard and soft supervision are locally similar but diverge under iteration. Rows denote model families and groups denote animal traits. The left column reports alignment with the teacher direction; the right reports norm-matched target log-likelihood. Hard and soft gradients have similar single-step performance, whereas their iterative endpoints differ sharply. The iterative results give the opposite impression. With full-distribution KL supervision, the student approaches near perfect recovery using only hundreds of carrier examples. This shows that, in our controlled setting, a small carrier set already contains enough information to identify Δ T \Delta_{T} ; tens of thousands of examples are not required merely to obtain adequate coverage. Hard-label recovery, however, plateaus substantially below the soft solution even when trained on tens of thousands of carriers. Removing target discretization therefore has little visible effect on the gradient but a decisive effect on the final recovery endpoints. These observations rule out either naive explanation in isolation. Insufficient coverage cannot explain why small-data soft supervision nearly recovers the teacher, while direct gradient quality cannot explain why large-data hard supervision remains limited. The resulting puzzle is: How can hard-label error be almost invisible in the local learning signal, yet dominate the endpoint of iterative subliminal learning? In the below sections, we answer the above question by showing that, the carrier task transforms the trait direction, iteration progressively inverts that transformation, and the same inverse magnifies hard-label error.

sections.heading: 6 Data Scale Controls the Depth of Hard-Label Inversion
sections.text: Section 5.2 shows that optimization progressively removes the carrier transformation, reaching flatter components only at later steps. Under hard supervision, however, each additional stage of inversion acts not only on the teacher signal but also on the fixed sampling error derived in Section 4.1 . Recovery therefore has a data-dependent optimal depth: early updates reduce carrier-induced bias, whereas sufficiently late updates amplify sampled-label error faster than they recover the remaining signal. We show that increasing the number of independent carriers postpones this crossover, allowing the student to follow the noiseless trajectory longer and recover progressively flatter components.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We asked whether subliminal learning requires large carrier datasets because the trait is insufficiently represented or because sampled targets introduce error. Controlled experiments show that hard and soft supervision produce nearly identical but distorted initial gradients, yet soft supervision recovers the teacher direction from hundreds of carriers while hard recovery remains limited. Our noisy-inverse model explains why: carrier Fisher geometry transforms the teacher direction, iteration reverses this transformation, and the same inverse amplifies fixed hard-label error, especially in weakly observed directions. Large datasets therefore make deeper inversion reliable rather than merely revealing an absent trait. This unifies the shared single-step ceiling, divergent iterative endpoints, and the advantage of new independent data over repeated passes on fixed samples.

sections.heading: Subliminal learning.
sections.text: Knowledge distillation conventionally transfers a teacher’s predictive behavior by matching its outputs ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) . Subliminal learning shows that model-generated data can additionally transmit behavioral traits that are not semantically expressed in those data ( Cloud et al., 2026 ) . Subsequent work has studied when this transfer occurs across architectures, carrier tasks, and intervention parameterizations ( Schrodi et al., 2025 ; Blank et al., 2026 ) . These studies establish the generality of hidden trait transfer, whereas we focus on the optimization geometry that determines how accurately a known trait direction can be recovered.

sections.heading: Steering-vector accounts.
sections.text: Recent work connects subliminal transfer to the distillation of latent steering directions ( Blank et al., 2026 ) and introduces subliminal steering as a controlled way to encode stronger, directly measurable hidden signals ( Morgulis and Hewitt, 2026 ) . We adopt this controlled setting because it exposes both the teacher direction and the recovered student direction. Our analysis complements these accounts by showing that the carrier task first transforms the teacher direction through its Fisher geometry and that iterative optimization acts as an increasingly strong inverse of that transformation.

sections.heading: Data scale and signal localization.
sections.text: Empirically, increasing the number of independently generated distillation examples makes latent teacher traits more recoverable ( Dong et al., 2026 ) . Related evidence emphasizes that independent carrier diversity is more useful than repeatedly training on a fixed dataset and links transfer to token positions at which teacher predictions diverge ( Feng, 2026 ) . These observations explain where trait-dependent signals can appear, but do not characterize why recovery continues to depend on large independent datasets after the mean learning direction has stabilized. Our noisy-inverse account separates these roles: carrier geometry determines the systematic transformation of the trait, while independent hard targets control the residual discretization error that is amplified as optimization inverts that transformation.

sections.heading: Inverse problems and iterative regularization.
sections.text: The locally linearized recovery dynamics are a finite-dimensional instance of Landweber iteration ( Landweber, 1951 ) : the iteration count acts as a regularization parameter, and each Fisher eigendirection is governed by a spectral filter. This perspective is classical in inverse problems ( Tikhonov and Arsenin, 1977 ; Engl et al., 1996 ; Hansen, 1998 ) , including the use of Tikhonov-style damping and early stopping to suppress unstable low-curvature modes. Statistical inverse-problem theory further characterizes the corresponding bias–variance tradeoff when the observation error is random and decreases with sample size ( Bissantz et al., 2007 ; Cavalier, 2008 ) . Our plots of trait energy across the Fisher spectrum are also related to spectral source and discrete Picard conditions, which describe how the target coefficients are distributed relative to an ill-posed operator’s spectrum ( Hansen, 1998 ) .

sections.heading: Spectral filtering and early stopping in learning.
sections.text: Gradient descent has likewise been studied as a spectral regularization method in learning theory ( Yao et al., 2007 ; Bauer et al., 2007 ; Lo Gerfo et al., 2008 ) . This literature establishes consistency and stopping rules for iterative regularization ( Raskutti et al., 2014 ) , relates gradient-flow paths to ridge regularization ( Ali et al., 2019 ) , and analyzes mode-dependent learning and overtraining in high-dimensional models ( Advani et al., 2020 ) . Our contribution is therefore not the general observation that gradient descent implements a spectral filter. We identify the carrier Fisher as the relevant forward operator for subliminal steering, derive the hard-label forcing term and its sample-size dependence, and test the resulting mode-wise and data-scaling predictions in an auditable parameter-recovery setting.

sections.heading: Fisher geometry and distributional supervision.
sections.text: Fisher preconditioning is central to natural-gradient methods ( Amari, 1998 ) ; importantly, the model Fisher used here is distinct from the observed-label outer product often called the empirical Fisher ( Kunstner et al., 2019 ) . Prior statistical accounts of knowledge distillation show that replacing sampled hard labels with teacher probabilities can reduce the variance of the student objective ( Menon et al., 2021 ) . In our setting, this variance reduction has a specific inverse-problem consequence: distributional supervision retains the carrier-transformed signal while removing the conditional token-sampling noise that would otherwise be amplified along low-curvature directions.

sections.heading: Appendix D Limitations and future work
sections.text: Our analysis is local. It linearizes the model around the unsteered state and treats the carrier Fisher matrix F F as approximately constant along the bounded recovery trajectory. This approximation captures the observed curvature-dependent ordering of recovery, but changes in the model Jacobian and Fisher geometry can account for deviations from the fixed- F F dynamics. We use subliminal steering as an experimental platform because it turns hidden trait transfer into an auditable parameter-recovery problem: both the implanted teacher direction and the recovered student direction are known, so recovery can be measured directly rather than inferred only from behavior. Representing the teacher trait by a single low-dimensional steering vector also makes an explicit Fisher analysis computationally feasible. This control does not cover the full range of subliminal learning. Traits induced by system prompts and students trained through LoRA or full-parameter fine-tuning may involve larger, higher-dimensional, and more nonlinear changes than the bounded steering trajectories studied here. Whether the same noise-dominated inverse mechanism accounts for their data requirements therefore remains to be tested across broader teacher constructions, student parameterizations, and carrier tasks; we leave those further validations for future work.

We ask where this data requirement comes from. Our testbed is subliminal steering: the teacher trait is a known residual-stream vector Δ T \Delta_{T} , so transfer can be measured directly as parameter recovery. On identical carrier prefixes, we compare token-level (hard) NLL supervision with full-distribution (soft) KL supervision. At initialization the two objectives give nearly collinear gradients, and both align poorly with Δ T \Delta_{T} . Under iterative optimization, however, they diverge: soft supervision recovers Δ T \Delta_{T} almost exactly from a few hundred carriers, while hard supervision stays well below it even with tens of thousands. We explain this gap by casting steering-vector distillation as a noisy linear inverse problem. Locally, the carrier task maps the trait through its Fisher matrix F F , so gradients point toward F ​ Δ T F\Delta_{T} rather than Δ T \Delta_{T} . Gradient descent then acts as a progressively less-damped inverse of F F . With soft targets, this inverse restores low-curvature directions. With hard labels, it also amplifies the sampling noise in those same directions. The result is an optimal inversion depth that grows with the number of independent carriers. Experiments on Qwen2.5-7B and Gemma-2-9B confirm four predictions: the Fisher distortion of the initial gradient, recovery ordered from steep to flat directions, an optimal depth that shifts with data scale, and the finding that resampling completions from a fixed prompt pool works as well as adding new prompts. In this setting, large carrier datasets are needed less to reveal the trait than to suppress label noise amplified by Fisher inversion. Code is available at https://github.com/luoyuchenmlcv/subliminal-data . 1 Introduction Model distillation trains a student to imitate a teacher’s outputs ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) . Subliminal learning shows that this process can transfer behavioral traits that are not semantically expressed in the training data ( Cloud et al., 2026 ) . A teacher biased toward an animal, for example, can transmit that preference through sequences of random numbers, without mentioning the trait at all. Subliminal transfers have also been observed across carrier tasks, model families, and trait types ( Cloud et al., 2026 ; Schrodi et al., 2025 ; Blank et al., 2026 ; Morgulis and Hewitt, 2026 ) . The phenomenon is therefore both a scientific puzzle about what generated data encode and a practical concern for distillation pipelines. Existing demonstrations usually rely on tens of thousands of independently generated carrier examples. Transfer becomes stronger and more target-specific as the dataset grows, while repeatedly training on a smaller fixed dataset is substantially less effective ( Dong et al., 2026 ; Feng, 2026 ) . This dependence admits two candidate explanations. Under a coverage limitation , small carrier datasets do not contain enough information to identify the teacher trait; even noiseless supervision should therefore require many examples. Under a noise limitation , the trait is already identifiable from a much smaller carrier set, but sampled hard targets provide a noisy estimate of the teacher distribution; replacing them with distributional supervision should substantially improve the learning signal or its final recovery. Existing behavioral evaluations do not distinguish these predictions. We test these explanations in the subliminal-steering framework ( Morgulis and Hewitt, 2026 ) . The teacher trait is represented by a known residual-stream vector Δ T \Delta_{T} , and the student learns a vector Δ S \Delta_{S} from carrier data generated by the steered teacher. Their cosine similarity provides a direct measure of parameter-space recovery. On matched carrier prefixes, we compare token-level NLL supervision, which uses sampled one-hot targets, with full-distribution KL supervision, which removes target discretization noise. We examine this intervention at two levels. Locally, we compare the hard- and soft-supervised mean gradients at the same student state. Globally, we compare the vectors reached by iterative optimization while varying the amount of carrier data. The results create a two-sided contradiction. With sufficiently many carriers, the hard- and soft-supervised mean gradients are nearly collinear, yet both have similarly low alignment with Δ T \Delta_{T} . Iterative optimization gives the opposite impression. Distributional supervision recovers Δ T \Delta_{T} almost perfectly from only hundreds of examples, showing that large-scale carrier coverage is unnecessary in this controlled setting. Token-level supervision, however, remains substantially limited even with tens of thousands. Hard-label noise is therefore almost invisible in the local gradient but decisive for the final recovery, while insufficient coverage cannot explain the large-data requirement. Controlled experiments show that hard and soft supervision produce nearly identical but distorted initial gradients, yet soft supervision recovers the teacher direction from hundreds of carriers while hard recovery remains limited. Our noisy-inverse model explains why: carrier Fisher geometry transforms the teacher direction, iteration reverses this transformation, and the same inverse amplifies fixed hard-label error, especially in weakly observed directions. Large datasets therefore make deeper inversion reliable rather than merely revealing an absent trait. This unifies the shared single-step ceiling, divergent iterative endpoints, and the advantage of new independent data over repeated passes on fixed samples.
